notes: reading: Rent and farm rent are qualified business income only when the person states the unadjusted basis of qualified property (not the SSTB basis) and no other trade or business (self-employment, farm operations, partnership or S corporation income): qualified property is by definition held by a qualified trade or business (26 U.S.C. 199A(b)(6)(A)), and when the person's only stated activities that could hold it are rentals, the rentals are that business. Otherwise whether a rental is a section 162 trade or business (199A(d)(1); Treas. Reg. 1.199A-1(b)(14); the 250 hours of Rev. Proc. 2019-38) is not stated, so it is not. Estate income is not qualified business income. Tax-Calculator gets a qualified rental in e27200 (with e02000) and any other rental in e02000 only; TAXSIM gets a qualified rental in `scorp` and any other rental and estate income in `intrec`. Alternatives: no rental is qualified (the basis left without effect), or every rental is (policyengine-us's default: rental_income_would_be_qualified and farm_rent_income_would_be_qualified default to true).

reading: A filer with a 401(k) deferral (traditional or Roth) is an active participant in an employer plan for the IRA deduction limit (26 U.S.C. 219(g)(5)); a filer with none is not, since no other plan coverage is stated.
itemized_notes: reading: Stated other health insurance premiums are not counted again: policyengine-us documents them as part of the stated premiums without Medicare Part B (variables/household/expense/health/other_health_insurance_premiums.py), so counting both would double count. Medical expenses take the premiums without Medicare Part B.

reading: Stated charitable gifts go to public charities (170(b)(1)(A) organizations): a private foundation is not stated. Non-cash gifts are ordinary-income property, deductible at the stated amount up to 50% of the contribution base less the cash allowed (170(b)(1)(A), (G)(iii)): no appreciation is stated, so none is capital gain property (170(b)(1)(C)). Cash counts up to 60% (170(b)(1)(G)); from 2026 only the total above 0.5% of the contribution base counts (170(b)(1)(I)). The excess over a ceiling carries forward five years; none is stated as carried in. Tax-Calculator applies its own ceilings (30% for non-cash gifts, 60% in all, after the floor); a note names a difference.
reading: Over-the-counter health expenses are left out of medical expenses: the stated amount is not said to be prescribed medicine or insulin (26 U.S.C. 213(b)) or other medical care (213(d)(1)).
